claims.statement: A general-purpose language model can be successfully trained through distillation during pretraining.
The student retains BERT's general architecture, removes token-type embeddings and the pooler, and reduces the number of layers by a factor of two.
The authors report that their distilled models require a smaller computational training budget than their larger counterparts.
The final training objective linearly combines teacher-distribution distillation, masked language modeling, and cosine embedding losses.

The distillation component trains the student on the teacher's soft target probabilities, using the same softmax temperature for teacher and student during training and a temperature of one at inference.
The cosine embedding loss is intended to align the directions of student and teacher hidden-state vectors, and the authors report that adding it is beneficial.
DistilBERT is 40% smaller than BERT.
DistilBERT retains 97% of BERT's language understanding capabilities.
DistilBERT is 60% faster than BERT.
The authors report that ablation studies indicate all three components of the triple loss are important for obtaining the best performance.
The authors claim that their compressed models can run on mobile devices and that on-device capabilities are demonstrated through a proof-of-concept experiment and a comparative on-device study.
The student is initialized from the teacher by taking one layer out of every two, using their shared dimensionality.
DistilBERT is distilled using gradient accumulation for batches of up to 4,000 examples, dynamic masking, and no next sentence prediction objective.
The pretrained model is fine-tuned separately on the nine GLUE datasets and evaluated on their development sets without ensembling or multitask fine-tuning.
SQuAD adaptation can include a second distillation stage using a BERT teacher already fine-tuned on SQuAD, following the pretraining distillation stage.
For the additional SQuAD adaptation-distillation setting, the prose reports 79.8 F1 and 70.4 exact match, described by the authors as within three points of the full model.
The ablation reference model uses a triple loss with components labeled Lce, Lcos, and Lmlm, together with teacher-weight initialization.
The authors report that DistilBERT matches or improves on the ELMo baseline across all nine GLUE tasks.

On IMDb, DistilBERT is reported to trail BERT by 0.6 percentage points in test accuracy while being 40% smaller; on SQuAD, the prose reports a gap of at most 3.9 points without specifying the metric in that statement.

For a complete pass over the STS-B development set on an Intel Xeon E5-2690 v3 Haswell CPU at 2.9 GHz with batch size one, the authors report that DistilBERT has 40% fewer parameters and is 60% faster than BERT.
The extracted ablation table reports GLUE macro-score changes of -2.96 without Lce, -1.46 without Lcos, and -0.31 without Lmlm, relative to the triple-loss model initialized with teacher weights.
The extracted ablation table reports a 3.69-point reduction in GLUE macro-score when the triple-loss model uses random initialization rather than teacher-weight initialization.

In a question answering application on an iPhone 7 Plus, DistilBERT is reported to be 71% faster than the authors' BERT-base question answering model when tokenization is excluded, with a model storage size of 207 MB.
Removing the masked language modeling component from the full triple loss has little impact on the distilled model's GLUE macro-score.
The two distillation losses account for a large portion of the distilled model's performance in the GLUE macro-score ablation.
Using the teacher's knowledge through additional distillation signals during pretraining is beneficial.
The ablation study evaluates the influence of triple-loss components and student initialization using GLUE macro-scores and deltas relative to the full triple loss.
Leveraging teacher knowledge through initialization and additional losses leads to substantial performance gains.
DistilBERT is a compelling option for edge applications.
